original_question: What is the computational complexity of the collection algorithm used to compute normal forms of elements in polycyclic groups?
target_in_paper: Section 11, Open Problems, "Complexity Analysis and Security," item 3: "What is the complexity of the collection algorithm to find the normal form of elements in polycyclic groups?" ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the exact algorithmic object (the collection algorithm), the exact group class (polycyclic groups), and the exact type of issue the paper asks about (complexity of computing normal forms). It is already very close to the paper's official open problem. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
missing_details: The paper asks this in the setting of a polycyclic group given by a consistent polycyclic presentation; section 8 defines the collection algorithm only in that presentation-theoretic setting. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
The input is not an abstract element but a word in the chosen generators of the presentation. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
The output is the unique normal form of the represented element. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The normal form is the standard polycyclic normal word (with integer exponents and, for torsion indices, bounded exponents), but your draft does not state that representation. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The algorithm is described as repeatedly applying the power and conjugacy relations of the presentation to subwords until the normal form is reached; that operational content is implicit in the paper's question and absent from the draft. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

Section 8 makes explicit that this is the mechanism used to solve the word problem in consistent polycyclic presentations, so the word-problem connection is part of the nearby intended scope. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The draft does not specify the complexity parameters. To be stand-alone, the question should make clear that complexity is being asked as a function of the input word length and the underlying presentation data. This parameterization is natural but not spelled out in the paper. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The paper does not explicitly say whether 'complexity' here means worst-case, average-case, or generic-case complexity; section 9 distinguishes these notions, and section 11 separately asks a generic-case question for a different problem, so this open problem should remain the unqualified collection-algorithm complexity question rather than be broadened. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The surrounding motivation is cryptographic: platform groups should have efficiently computable normal forms. Your draft omits that nearby intent, though it is part of why this open problem is posed. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
refined_question: Given a polycyclic group G specified by a consistent polycyclic presentation, and a word w in the generators of that presentation, what is the computational complexity of the collection algorithm that repeatedly applies the presentation's power and conjugacy relations to rewrite w to the unique polycyclic normal form of the element represented by w? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently: for a polycyclic group given by a consistent polycyclic presentation, what is the complexity of solving the word problem by computing unique normal forms via the collection algorithm? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
justification: This is the nearest official formulation because section 11 states it verbatim as an open problem under "Complexity Analysis and Security." Section 8 supplies the exact local context needed to sharpen it without broadening it: every polycyclic group has a consistent polycyclic presentation, every element then has a unique normal form, and the collection algorithm computes that normal form from a word in the generators by repeated use of power and conjugacy relations, thereby solving the word problem. Section 7 explains why efficiently computable normal forms matter for cryptographic platform groups, and section 9 separately distinguishes worst-case, average-case, and generic complexity, which is why the question should not be rewritten as a neighboring conjugacy-problem question or as a generic-complexity question. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
